dryRun.title: Count islands (1 = land) in the grid  1 1 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 1
dryRun.note: A grid is a graph: each cell is a node, and its neighbours are the cells up, down, left and right. Scan every cell. When you find land that is not marked, count one island and flood-fill it so it is never counted again.

think.q:
const g = [[1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]
let count = 0
const dfs = (r, c) => {
  if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] !== 1) return
  g[r][c] = 2
  dfs(r + 1, c); dfs(r - 1, c); dfs(r, c + 1); dfs(r, c - 1)
}
for (let r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
  for (let c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
    if (g[r][c] === 1) { count++; dfs(r, c) }
console.log(count)
why: The cells (0,0), (0,1) and (1,1) touch and form one island. The cell (2,2) touches nothing but a corner, and corners do not count. That is a second island.
Writing 2 into a visited cell is the "mark as seen" step, so the cell is skipped later.

think.q:
const dirs = [[1, 0], [-1, 0], [0, 1], [0, -1]]
const inside = (r, c) => r >= 0 && c >= 0 && r < 3 && c < 3
const nb = (r, c) => dirs.filter(([dr, dc]) => inside(r + dr, c + dc)).length
console.log(nb(0, 0), nb(1, 1))
why: A corner cell has only 2 neighbours inside a 3 × 3 grid, and the centre has 4.
Keeping the four directions in a list (dirs) avoids four copy-pasted lines, and a single inside check avoids out-of-range reads.
think.exec:
const dirs = [[1, 0], [-1, 0], [0, 1], [0, -1]]
const inside = (r, c) => r >= 0 && c >= 0 && r < 3 && c < 3
const nb = (r, c) => dirs.filter(([dr, dc]) => inside(r + dr, c + dc)).length
console.log(nb(0, 0), nb(1, 1))

think.q:
const g = [[1]]
try {
  console.log(g[-1][0])
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.constructor.name)
}
why: g[-1] is undefined, and reading [0] of undefined throws a TypeError. Always check the row before touching the cell.
In the check, test the row and column ranges first, and the cell value last.

think.q: A grid has R rows and C columns. What is the time of the island count?
why: Every cell is scanned once, and every land cell is flood-filled once because it is marked right away.
The marks are the reason it does not blow up to the square.

think.q: "Rotting oranges": every minute, fresh oranges next to a rotten one become rotten. How many minutes until all are rotten? Which tool fits?
opts: DFS from the first rotten orange
BFS that starts with all rotten oranges in the queue at once (multi-source BFS)
why: The rot spreads at the same time from all rotten cells, one ring per minute. That is a BFS with many starting points, counted level by level.
"Nearest X" or "time to spread" in a grid usually means BFS.

try.task: Write numIslands(grid). grid is an array of rows with 1 (land) and 0 (water). An island is land cells joined up, down, left or right (not diagonally). Return the number of islands. Do not change the input. It must work on a 300 × 300 grid of all land.
try.hint: Copy the grid (or keep a seen array). Scan each cell. For unseen land, count 1 and flood-fill with your own stack, because recursion goes 90,000 calls deep on a big island.

checks.verify: assert(numIslands([[1, 0], [0, 1]]) === 2, "expected 2")

checks.t: no land and an empty grid
checks.verify: assert(numIslands([[0, 0], [0, 0]]) === 0 && numIslands([]) === 0, "expected 0")
const g = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]; numIslands(g); assert(JSON.stringify(g) === "[[1,1],[0,1]]", "the input was changed")
const g = Array.from({ length: 300 }, () => new Array(300).fill(1)); assert(numIslands(g) === 1, "expected 1")

takeaway.key: A grid is a graph with up to 4 neighbours per cell. Scan every cell, and flood-fill each new piece of land once: O(R × C). Check the bounds first. Use BFS for "nearest" and "spread over time".
mistakes: Not marking cells as seen, so the fill never ends.
Deep recursion on a big island (use an explicit stack).

dryRun.title: Union-find on 5 nodes. Each node starts as its own root.
rows: 3 groups: root of 2 now points at root 0
1 group: root 3 now points at root 0
dryRun.note: Each group is a tree, and its root is the group name. find(x) walks up to the root. union(a, b) joins the two roots. Two nodes are connected exactly when their roots are equal.

think.q:
const parent = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
const find = (x) => (parent[x] === x ? x : (parent[x] = find(parent[x])))
const union = (a, b) => {
  const ra = find(a), rb = find(b)
  if (ra === rb) return false
  parent[rb] = ra
  return true
}
union(0, 1); union(1, 2); union(3, 4)
console.log(find(0) === find(2), find(0) === find(4), new Set(parent.map((_, i) => find(i))).size)
why: 0, 1 and 2 are one group, and 3 and 4 are another. So 0 and 2 are connected, 0 and 4 are not, and there are 2 groups (2 different roots).
The number of groups equals the number of different roots.

think.q:
const parent = [0, 0, 1, 2]   // a chain 3 → 2 → 1 → 0
const find = (x) => (parent[x] === x ? x : (parent[x] = find(parent[x])))
find(3)
console.log(parent.join(","))
why: While walking up to the root, find re-points every node on the path straight at the root. The chain becomes flat.
This is path compression. The next find on any of these nodes takes one step.
think.exec:
const parent = [0, 0, 1, 2]   // a chain 3 → 2 → 1 → 0
const find = (x) => (parent[x] === x ? x : (parent[x] = find(parent[x])))
find(3)
console.log(parent.join(","))

think.q: You process the edges of an undirected graph one by one with union(a, b). When does an edge create a cycle?
opts: When a and b are both roots
When find(a) and find(b) are already the same (union returns false)
When a is smaller than b
When the group count goes up
why: If a and b are already in the same group, there is already a path between them. Adding this edge closes a loop.
This is how Kruskal's algorithm skips edges that would make a cycle.

think.q: With path compression (and union by size or rank), how long does one find or union take, roughly?
why: The inverse Ackermann function grows so slowly that it is at most 4 or 5 for any real input. In practice it is constant.
Without either trick, a long chain makes find cost O(n).

think.q: Which question is a natural fit for union-find?
opts: Are these two people in the same friend group, while friendships keep being added?
Find the median of a stream
why: Union-find answers "same group?" very fast while groups merge over time. It never splits groups.
Other uses: number of components as edges arrive, Kruskal's MST, "accounts merge".

try.task: Write createUnionFind(n) for nodes 0 to n - 1. It returns an object with find(x) (the root of x), union(a, b) (join the groups, return true if they were different and false if they were already joined), connected(a, b) and count() (the number of groups). It must handle 100,000 nodes joined in a long chain.
try.hint: Keep parent and a size array. Write find with a loop (path halving: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]) so a deep chain cannot overflow the stack. Attach the smaller tree under the bigger one.

checks.verify: const uf = createUnionFind(5); uf.union(0, 1); uf.union(1, 2); assert(uf.connected(0, 2) === true && uf.connected(0, 4) === false && uf.count() === 3, "connected or count is wrong")

checks.t: union tells whether it joined anything
checks.verify: const uf = createUnionFind(3); assert(uf.union(0, 1) === true && uf.union(1, 0) === false && uf.union(0, 1) === false, "union return values")
const uf = createUnionFind(4); assert(uf.count() === 4 && uf.find(2) === 2 && uf.connected(1, 1) === true, "start state")

checks.t: groups merge through a shared member
checks.verify: const uf = createUnionFind(6); uf.union(0, 1); uf.union(2, 3); uf.union(1, 3); assert(uf.connected(0, 2) && !uf.connected(0, 4) && uf.count() === 3, "merge groups")

checks.t: 100,000 nodes in a long chain (a recursive find would crash)
checks.verify: const n = 100000; const uf = createUnionFind(n); for (let i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) uf.union(i + 1, i); assert(uf.connected(0, n - 1) && uf.count() === 1, "chain of 100,000 failed")

takeaway.key: Union-find keeps groups as trees. find returns the root; union joins two roots. With path compression and union by size both are almost O(1). If union returns false, the edge makes a cycle.
mistakes: Comparing the nodes instead of their roots.
Recursive find on a huge chain (use a loop).
Linking nodes instead of roots in union.
Forgetting to lower the group count only when a real join happens.

dryRun.title: Kahn's algorithm. Edges 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1. In-degrees: 0:2, 1:2, 2:1, 3:1, 4:0, 5:0
dryRun.note: Start with every node that has no incoming edge. Take one, add it to the order, and remove its outgoing edges (lower the in-degree of its neighbours). Any neighbour that reaches 0 can go next.

think.q:
const n = 6
const edges = [[5, 2], [5, 0], [4, 0], [4, 1], [2, 3], [3, 1]]
const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => [])
const indeg = new Array(n).fill(0)
for (const [a, b] of edges) { adj[a].push(b); indeg[b]++ }
const q = []
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] === 0) q.push(i)
const order = []
while (q.length) {
  const u = q.shift()
  order.push(u)
  for (const v of adj[u]) if (--indeg[v] === 0) q.push(v)
}
console.log(order.join(","))
why: Nodes 4 and 5 have no incoming edges, so they start in the queue. After 5 is taken, both 2 and 0 are released, and so on.
Other valid orders exist (for example 5,4,2,3,1,0). Every edge just needs its source before its target.

think.q:
const n = 3
const edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 1]]
const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => [])
const indeg = new Array(n).fill(0)
for (const [a, b] of edges) { adj[a].push(b); indeg[b]++ }
const q = [], order = []
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] === 0) q.push(i)
while (q.length) {
  const u = q.shift()
  order.push(u)
  for (const v of adj[u]) if (--indeg[v] === 0) q.push(v)
}
console.log(order.length)
why: Nodes 1 and 2 point at each other, so neither ever reaches in-degree 0. Only node 0 gets out.
If order.length < n, the graph has a cycle and there is no valid order. This is how you detect an impossible course plan.

think.q: What makes an ordering of the nodes a valid topological order?
opts: It is sorted by node number
For every edge u → v, u appears before v
Every node appears next to its neighbours
why: The order respects every "must come before" rule. There is often more than one valid order, so a test must check the rule, not one exact list.
Only a directed graph without cycles (a DAG) has one.

think.q: What is the time of Kahn's algorithm?
why: Every node is queued once and every edge is removed once.
The same bound holds for the DFS version.

think.q: With DFS you can also build a topological order. What do you do?
opts: Record each node when you first reach it
Record each node after all its neighbours are done (postorder), then reverse the list
why: A node is finished only after everything it points to is finished. So finishing order is "targets first", and reversing it puts sources first.
Both versions are fine. Kahn's is easier to explain and detects cycles for free.

try.task: Write courseOrder(n, prerequisites). There are n courses (0 to n - 1). Each pair [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. Return any valid order that takes all courses, or [] if it is impossible (a cycle).
try.hint: Build the graph with an edge b → a for each pair, and count the in-degree of every course. Queue the courses with in-degree 0. Pop, record, lower the in-degree of its targets, and queue those that reach 0. At the end, if you recorded fewer than n, return [].

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(courseOrder(2, [[1, 0]])) === "[0,1]", "expected [0,1]")

checks.t: a cycle gives an empty list
checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(courseOrder(2, [[1, 0], [0, 1]])) === "[]", "expected []")

const pre = [[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]]; const o = courseOrder(4, pre); assert(o.length === 4 && new Set(o).size === 4, "must contain every course once"); for (const [a, b] of pre) assert(o.indexOf(b) < o.indexOf(a), "course " + b + " must come before " + a)
const o = courseOrder(3, []); assert(o.length === 3 && new Set(o).size === 3, "expected all three courses")

const n = 50000; const pre = Array.from({ length: n - 1 }, (_, i) => [i + 1, i]); const o = courseOrder(n, pre); let ok = o.length === n; for (let i = 0; i < n && ok; i++) if (o[i] !== i) ok = false; assert(ok, "wrong order for the long chain")

takeaway.key: Topological sort orders a directed acyclic graph so every edge points forward. Kahn's way: queue the in-degree 0 nodes, remove their edges, repeat. If you place fewer than n nodes, there is a cycle. O(V + E).
mistakes: Reversing the edge direction (a prerequisite pair [a, b] is an edge b → a).
Forgetting to detect the cycle by comparing the order length with n.
Testing for one exact order when many are valid.
Using it on an undirected graph.

dryRun.title: Dijkstra from node 0. Edges 0→1 (4), 0→2 (1), 2→1 (2), 1→3 (1), 2→3 (5)
dryRun.note: Always finish the node with the smallest known distance. Its distance can no longer improve (weights are not negative). Then relax its edges: if going through it is shorter, update the neighbour.

think.q:
const n = 4
const edges = [[0, 1, 4], [0, 2, 1], [2, 1, 2], [1, 3, 1], [2, 3, 5]]
const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => [])
for (const [u, v, w] of edges) adj[u].push([v, w])
const dist = Array(n).fill(Infinity)
dist[0] = 0
const done = Array(n).fill(false)
for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) {
  let u = -1
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (!done[i] && (u === -1 || dist[i] < dist[u])) u = i
  if (dist[u] === Infinity) break
  done[u] = true
  for (const [v, w] of adj[u]) if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) dist[v] = dist[u] + w
}
console.log(dist.join(","))
why: The cheapest way to node 1 is 0 → 2 → 1, which costs 1 + 2 = 3, not the direct edge of 4. The cheapest way to node 3 is 0 → 2 → 1 → 3, costing 4.
This version picks the next node by scanning all nodes, which is O(V²). A heap makes the pick O(log V).

think.q: Edge 0→1 costs 4, but 0→2→1 costs 1 + 2 = 3. Why does BFS give the wrong answer here?
opts: BFS counts edges, not weights, so it prefers the path with fewer edges even if it is more expensive
why: BFS finds the path with the fewest edges: 0→1 has 1 edge. Dijkstra finds the cheapest total weight: 0→2→1.
If all weights are equal, BFS and Dijkstra give the same answer.

think.q: Why does Dijkstra break when an edge has a negative weight?
opts: A node it already finished could later become cheaper through the negative edge, but it never looks at it again
It loops forever on every graph
why: The key promise is "the closest unfinished node is final". A negative edge can break this promise.
For negative weights use Bellman-Ford (next lessons).

think.q: With a heap, the same node can be pushed several times as its distance improves. When you pop [d, u] and d > dist[u], what do you do?
opts: Skip it, it is an old entry
why: A better distance for u was already found and processed. This entry is out of date.
This "lazy deletion" is simpler than removing items from the middle of a heap.

think.q: What is the time of Dijkstra with a binary heap?
why: Each edge can push one heap entry, and each push or pop costs O(log V). That is E log V, plus V log V for the pops.
The simple scan version is O(V²), which is fine for small dense graphs.

try.task: Write dijkstra(n, edges, start). The graph is directed, with nodes 0 to n - 1, and each edge is [from, to, weight] with a weight of 0 or more. Return an array of the shortest distance from start to every node, using Infinity for unreachable nodes. It must handle 50,000 nodes.
try.hint: Keep a min-heap of [distance, node] pairs (write a small one). Pop the smallest; skip it if d > dist[u]; otherwise relax each edge and push improved neighbours.

checks.verify: const d = dijkstra(3, [[0, 1, 5]], 0); assert(d[0] === 0 && d[1] === 5 && d[2] === Infinity, "expected [0,5,Infinity]")

checks.t: the cheaper of two parallel edges
checks.verify: const d = dijkstra(2, [[0, 1, 9], [0, 1, 3]], 0); assert(d[1] === 3, "expected 3")

checks.t: zero weights and a different start
checks.verify: const d = dijkstra(3, [[1, 2, 0], [2, 0, 4]], 1); assert(JSON.stringify(d) === "[4,0,0]", "expected [4,0,0]")

checks.t: a chain of 50,000 nodes stays fast
checks.verify: const n = 50000; const e = Array.from({ length: n - 1 }, (_, i) => [i, i + 1, (i % 3) + 1]); const t0 = Date.now(); const d = dijkstra(n, e, 0); assert(d[n - 1] === 99997 && Date.now() - t0 < 1500, "wrong distance or too slow, use a heap")

takeaway.key: Dijkstra finds shortest paths with non-negative weights: repeatedly finish the closest unfinished node and relax its edges. With a heap it is O((V + E) log V). Skip stale heap entries. Negative weights need Bellman-Ford.
mistakes: Using it with negative edge weights.
Using BFS when edges have different weights.
Forgetting to skip old heap entries (d > dist[u]).

flags: topological-sort: the try-it checks the rule (every prerequisite before its course), not an exact list, because many orders are valid.
union-find: the 100,000 node check unions in reverse order, which builds a long chain unless union by size is used. The reference also uses an iterative find.
dijkstra: the chain check compares an exact distance computed in the generator (weights 1, 2, 3 repeating).
grid-problems: the 300 x 300 check would overflow a recursive flood fill on most engines.
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (concept dry runs are not machine-run).
